title: Rotation changes nothing
summary: The same relationships can be drawn many ways. Rotate nodes, compare styles and learn that the order of tips on the page carries no meaning — on a tree of apes.

objectives: See that rotating a node changes the drawing, never the relationships
Recognise the same relationships drawn in different styles
Reject the idea that one tip is more evolved than another

items.text: Do these two trees show the same relationships, or does one show something different?
items.note_after: Reordering the branches at a node — rotating it — changes the drawing, never the relationships.

items.text: One of these trees shows different relationships from the other two. Rotate nodes freely — which tree is it?
Select every true statement. The node letters are on the first tree.

statements.text: The first and second trees show the same relationships.
The first and third trees show the same relationships.
Node R is older than node P.
Node P is older than node Q.

items.text: These two trees are drawn differently. Do they show the same relationships — and why?

reasons: They place every split among the same groups of taxa — rotating a node changes the drawing, never the relationships.
Their tips are drawn in a different order, so their relationships must differ.

items.text: On a phylogenetic tree, which tip is the most evolved?
items.note_after: Every tip is a present-day lineage; there is no 'advanced' or 'primitive' end of a tree.

options: No tip — every lineage has been evolving for the same total time since the root
The tip that branched off earliest
The tip whose ancestors branched most often
